Ferritin is adequate and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Spectrum bias arises when the included patient spectrum does not represent the population in which the test will be used. The study instead enrolls consecutive clinically relevant patients; the defining defect is selective application of the reference standard.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Differential verification bias occurs when different reference standards are used for different participants, often according to the index-test result. Here, coronary angiography is the only reference standard; the problem is that many index-negative participants are not verified at all.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. This study has partial verification bias, also called workup bias. Whether a participant receives the reference standard depends strongly on the index-test result: nearly all index-positive participants are verified, whereas most index-negative participants are not. Disease status is therefore known in a nonrandom subset of the tested cohort, which can bias estimated sensitivity and specificity.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Incorporation bias occurs when the index-test result forms part of the reference standard used to define disease. Here, angiography is prespecified independently and does not incorporate the blood-test result.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Reference-standard review bias occurs when interpretation of the reference standard is influenced by knowledge of the index test. The angiographers are explicitly blinded.

item.tested_construct: Diagnostic accuracy is biased when receipt of the reference standard depends on the index-test result, so disease status is verified in a nonrandom subset of tested participants.
item.vignette: Investigators prospectively enroll consecutive adults being evaluated for coronary artery disease and perform a new blood-based index test on every participant. Coronary angiography is the single prespecified reference standard. All participants with a positive index test undergo angiography, but because angiography is invasive, only a small random sample of participants with a negative index test undergo it. Sensitivity and specificity are then estimated only from participants whose disease status was verified by angiography. Angiographers are blinded to the index-test result.

item.vignette: A 68-year-old woman is hospitalized for evaluation of unintentional weight loss. Biopsy confirms pancreatic adenocarcinoma. She is alert, medically stable, and has decision-making capacity. Before the physician discusses the biopsy result with her, her adult children ask to speak privately. They say, “In our family, serious diagnoses are told to the eldest child first. Please do not tell our mother; it will make her lose hope.” The patient has never stated how she wants serious medical information communicated, and no immediate treatment decision is required.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration — Intralobar pulmonary sequestration is nonfunctioning dysplastic lung tissue without a normal tracheobronchial connection that lies within the visceral pleura of adjacent lung. It receives anomalous systemic arterial blood, most often from the descending thoracic aorta, and usually drains through the pulmonary veins.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Pulmonary arterial inflow with pulmonary venous drainage is the usual pulmonary circulation of functioning lung; a sequestration is defined by anomalous systemic arterial supply.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. The lesion is intralobar pulmonary sequestration because it is nonfunctioning lung without normal tracheobronchial communication and lies within the visceral pleura of the adjacent lung. Pulmonary sequestrations receive anomalous systemic arterial supply, most commonly from the descending thoracic aorta. Intralobar sequestrations usually drain through the pulmonary veins; in contrast, extralobar sequestrations have a separate pleural covering and more often drain through systemic veins such as the azygos or hemiazygos system.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Systemic arterial supply with systemic venous drainage is characteristic of extralobar sequestration more than intralobar sequestration. Extralobar lesions have their own pleural covering, whereas this lesion shares visceral pleura with adjacent lung.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Pulmonary arterial inflow is not the defining vascular supply of pulmonary sequestration, and systemic venous drainage would not match the usual intralobar pattern.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Although bronchial arteries are systemic vessels, the typical anomalous arterial supply of pulmonary sequestration arises from the descending thoracic aorta or another systemic artery, and intralobar lesions usually drain to pulmonary veins rather than directly to the superior vena cava.

Intralobar sequestrations usually drain through the pulmonary veins; in contrast, extralobar sequestrations have a separate pleural covering and more often drain through systemic veins such as the azygos or hemiazygos system.

Re-exposure to the corresponding minor red-cell antigen triggers a rapid secondary (anamnestic) antibody response, causing delayed destruction of transfused erythrocytes.

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. This is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. Remote transfusion can prime memory B cells against a minor red-cell antigen. Over time, the circulating alloantibody concentration may fall below the detection threshold of routine pretransfusion testing, so the current antibody screen and crossmatch can appear compatible. Re-exposure to antigen-positive donor erythrocytes then triggers an anamnestic antibody response, with delayed hemolysis and a newly positive direct antiglobulin test. Kidd-system antibodies are a classic cause because they can become difficult to detect between exposures and then rise rapidly after re-exposure.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. ABO-incompatible acute hemolytic transfusion reactions are driven by preexisting antibodies and occur during or soon after transfusion, not after a symptom-free interval of about a week with a newly detectable minor-antigen alloantibody.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies are associated with transfusion-related acute lung injury, which presents with acute hypoxemia and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than delayed DAT-positive hemolysis.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Anti-IgA-mediated reactions cause immediate allergic/anaphylactic manifestations in susceptible IgA-deficient recipients, not a delayed fall in hemoglobin with newly detectable anti-Jkᵃ.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease is caused by engrafted donor lymphocytes and produces a different syndrome, classically including fever, rash, gastrointestinal disease, liver injury, and marrow failure rather than isolated delayed alloimmune red-cell destruction.

item.vignette: A 51-year-old man who received packed red blood cells after trauma 7 years ago is admitted for gastrointestinal bleeding and receives crossmatch-compatible packed red blood cells. His pretransfusion antibody screen is negative. One week later, he has fatigue and mild jaundice. His hemoglobin has fallen toward the pretransfusion value, indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase are increased, and haptoglobin is decreased. The direct antiglobulin test is positive, and repeat antibody testing now detects anti-Jkᵃ.

Mutant NOTCH3 extracellular-domain material accumulates around vascular smooth muscle cells, with progressive mural-cell degeneration and dysfunction that predispose to migraine, subcortical ischemic events, white-matter disease, and cognitive decline.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy involves amyloid-beta deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels and typically predisposes to lobar hemorrhage. It does not explain this autosomal dominant syndrome of migraine with aura, early subcortical infarcts, and characteristic anterior temporal/external-capsule white-matter lesions.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. The combination of migraine with aura, early recurrent subcortical ischemic events, autosomal dominant family history, and white-matter hyperintensities involving the anterior temporal poles and external capsules strongly suggests CADASIL. CADASIL is caused by pathogenic NOTCH3 variants. The abnormal NOTCH3 extracellular domain accumulates in and around the walls of small arteries near vascular smooth muscle cells, where it is associated with progressive smooth-muscle-cell degeneration and cerebral small-vessel dysfunction. Skin-biopsy electron microscopy can show characteristic granular osmiophilic material near vascular smooth muscle cells.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. COL4A1-related small-vessel disease can cause hereditary cerebral arteriopathy and hemorrhage, but the classic CADASIL phenotype is caused by NOTCH3 pathology in vascular smooth muscle cells.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS cause stroke-like episodes that typically do not respect vascular territories and are accompanied by systemic mitochondrial features; the family pattern is usually maternal rather than autosomal dominant.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. ATP7B dysfunction causes Wilson disease with hepatic, psychiatric, and movement manifestations, not this inherited cerebral small-vessel pattern.

She has no diabetes mellitus and has normal blood pressure.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0609_Q0633_202609.claim: Amyloid-beta deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessel walls, causing vessel-wall fragility is incorrect for this vignette. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy involves amyloid-beta deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels and typically predisposes to lobar hemorrhage. It does not explain this autosomal dominant syndrome of migraine with aura, early subcortical infarcts, and characteristic anterior temporal/external-capsule white-matter lesions.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0609_Q0633_202609.target_mechanism: Pathogenic NOTCH3 variants cause an autosomal dominant cerebral small-vessel arteriopathy. Mutant NOTCH3 extracellular-domain material accumulates around vascular smooth muscle cells, with progressive mural-cell degeneration and dysfunction that predispose to migraine, subcortical ischemic events, white-matter disease, and cognitive decline.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0609_Q0633_202609.claim: Aggregation of mutant NOTCH3 extracellular-domain protein around vascular smooth muscle cells, causing small-artery degeneration is the uniquely best answer. The combination of migraine with aura, early recurrent subcortical ischemic events, autosomal dominant family history, and white-matter hyperintensities involving the anterior temporal poles and external capsules strongly suggests CADASIL. CADASIL is caused by pathogenic NOTCH3 variants. The abnormal NOTCH3 extracellular domain accumulates in and around the walls of small arteries near vascular smooth muscle cells, where it is associated with progressive smooth-muscle-cell degeneration and cerebral small-vessel dysfunction. Skin-biopsy electron microscopy can show characteristic granular osmiophilic material near vascular smooth muscle cells.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Pituitary apoplexy with acute secondary adrenal insufficiency — Sudden hemorrhage or infarction within the pituitary gland, often in a pre-existing adenoma, can abruptly impair ACTH secretion. The resulting cortisol deficiency reduces vascular responsiveness to vasoconstrictors and promotes nonosmotic ADH activity, causing hypotension and hyponatremia; aldosterone secretion is relatively preserved because it is regulated primarily by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and serum potassium.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. This patient has pituitary apoplexy: sudden hemorrhagic infarction of a pituitary macroadenoma causing abrupt headache, ophthalmoplegia, and endocrine failure. The most dangerous acute endocrine consequence is secondary adrenal insufficiency from loss of ACTH. Cortisol deficiency decreases vascular responsiveness to angiotensin II and catecholamines and can increase ADH-mediated water retention, producing hypotension and hyponatremia. Aldosterone is usually preserved because zona glomerulosa secretion is controlled mainly by the renin-angiotensin system and serum potassium rather than ACTH. Therefore potassium can remain normal, helping distinguish secondary from primary adrenal insufficiency.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary adrenal cortical destruction can cause cortisol and aldosterone deficiency with hyperkalemia and volume depletion. This patient has a pituitary lesion causing secondary adrenal insufficiency, in which aldosterone is generally preserved.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Loss of ADH causes central diabetes insipidus with polyuria and a tendency toward hypernatremia, not this hyponatremic pattern.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. TSH deficiency can contribute to chronic central hypothyroidism but does not explain the immediate life-threatening hypotension of acute pituitary apoplexy as directly as ACTH/cortisol loss.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Pituitary apoplexy causes loss rather than excess of ACTH in the relevant emergency. Excess cortisol would not produce the acute cortisol-deficient shock physiology shown.

explanation.educational_objective: In pituitary apoplexy, recognize acute ACTH deficiency as the critical cause of secondary adrenal insufficiency and distinguish it from primary adrenal failure by relative preservation of aldosterone and potassium balance.

item.difficulty_basis: Requires recognizing pituitary apoplexy and distinguishing secondary from primary adrenal insufficiency using potassium and aldosterone physiology.
item.lead_in: Which endocrine mechanism most directly explains this patient’s hemodynamic instability and electrolyte pattern?

options.A: Abrupt ACTH deficiency causing cortisol deficiency, with relatively preserved aldosterone secretion
options.B: Destruction of the adrenal cortex causing simultaneous cortisol and aldosterone deficiency
options.C: Loss of posterior pituitary ADH secretion causing renal free-water loss and hypovolemia
options.D: Abrupt TSH deficiency causing severe hypothyroidism as the primary cause of shock
options.E: Excess ACTH secretion causing cortisol-mediated suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

item.vignette: A 47-year-old man with a known nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma develops an abrupt severe retro-orbital headache, vomiting, diplopia, and left-sided ptosis. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L, potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, and glucose is 61 mg/dL. MRI shows acute hemorrhagic infarction within the pituitary mass with suprasellar expansion.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis — Neutralizing IgG autoantibodies against GM-CSF impair GM-CSF-dependent maturation and function of alveolar macrophages. The macrophages cannot adequately catabolize and clear surfactant from the alveolar surface, so lipoproteinaceous surfactant accumulates within alveoli and impairs gas exchange.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis reflects decreased clearance of surfactant rather than increased production. Type II pneumocyte hypersecretion is not the mechanism of autoimmune PAP.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Axonemal dynein defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia with impaired mucociliary clearance, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, and laterality abnormalities; they do not produce PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous alveolar filling.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease and impaired killing of catalase-positive organisms. Autoimmune PAP instead reflects dysfunctional alveolar macrophages from loss of effective GM-CSF signaling.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Dermatitis herpetiformis — Gluten-sensitive enteropathy can generate an IgA-dominant autoimmune response against transglutaminases. In dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermal transglutaminase 3 (TG3) is the dominant cutaneous autoantigen; IgA-TG3 immune deposits accumulate in the papillary dermis, recruit neutrophils, and produce intensely pruritic subepidermal vesicles.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Tissue transglutaminase/TG2 is the principal autoantigen of celiac enteropathy and circulating anti-TG2 antibodies are common in gluten-sensitive disease, but TG3 is the dominant cutaneous autoantigen in dermatitis herpetiformis.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Desmoglein 3 is a desmosomal cadherin targeted in pemphigus vulgaris, producing intraepidermal acantholysis and intercellular IgG rather than granular papillary IgA.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. BP180 is a hemidesmosomal protein targeted in bullous pemphigoid, which produces tense subepidermal bullae with linear IgG/C3 along the basement membrane rather than granular IgA at dermal papillae.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. The intensely pruritic symmetric eruption on extensor surfaces, neutrophils at dermal papillary tips, subepidermal vesicles, and granular IgA in the papillary dermis identify dermatitis herpetiformis. This disorder is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy even when gastrointestinal symptoms are absent. In celiac enteropathy, the dominant autoantigen is tissue transglutaminase (TG2). In dermatitis herpetiformis, epitope spreading produces high-affinity IgA against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3), and IgA-TG3 complexes localize in the papillary dermis and drive neutrophilic inflammation.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Type VII collagen is the anchoring-fibril target in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita; it does not produce the classic gluten-associated granular IgA pattern of dermatitis herpetiformis.

item.vignette: A 31-year-old man has several months of intensely pruritic, grouped papules and small vesicles on the extensor surfaces of both elbows, knees, and buttocks. Many lesions are excoriated. He has no chronic diarrhea or weight loss. Biopsy of an intact lesion shows neutrophils concentrated at the tips of dermal papillae with subepidermal vesicle formation. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits in the papillary dermis.

evidence_map.claim: Epidermal transglutaminase (transglutaminase 3): Correct. The intensely pruritic symmetric eruption on extensor surfaces, neutrophils at dermal papillary tips, subepidermal vesicles, and granular IgA in the papillary dermis identify dermatitis herpetiformis. In celiac enteropathy, the dominant autoantigen is tissue transglutaminase (TG2). In dermatitis herpetiformis, epitope spreading produces high-affinity IgA against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3), and IgA-TG3 complexes localize in the papillary dermis and drive neutrophilic inflammation.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Behçet syndrome — Behçet syndrome is a systemic autoinflammatory vasculitis capable of involving arteries and veins of variable caliber. Active lesions commonly show neutrophil-predominant vascular inflammation and thrombosis; the same inflammatory disease produces recurrent oral and genital aphthae, uveitis, pathergy, and arterial or venous vascular lesions.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells in medium and large arteries describes giant cell arteritis. Behçet syndrome is a variable-vessel disease involving both arteries and veins and does not require giant-cell granulomatous pathology.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. IgA vasculitis is an immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis that classically causes palpable purpura and can involve the kidneys, joints, and gastrointestinal tract. It does not explain the recurrent oral/genital aphthae, uveitis, pathergy, and variable-vessel thrombosis pattern.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically combines necrotizing granulomatous respiratory disease with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis; those findings are absent here.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with asthma, eosinophilia, and eosinophil-rich necrotizing granulomatous inflammation rather than the Behçet mucocutaneous-ocular-pathergy syndrome.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. Recurrent oral aphthae, scar-forming genital ulcers, uveitis, a positive pathergy reaction, and venous thrombosis identify Behçet syndrome. Behçet is unusual among vasculitides because it can affect both arteries and veins of all sizes. Histopathology commonly shows vascular inflammation with a prominent neutrophilic reaction and thrombosis. Venous thrombosis is a well-recognized vascular manifestation, while arterial disease can produce occlusions or aneurysms, including pulmonary artery aneurysms.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Ebstein anomaly — Failure of normal delamination of the septal and posterior tricuspid valve leaflets from the right ventricular myocardium causes apical displacement of the valve. The proximal portion of the right ventricle becomes functionally incorporated into the right atrium ('atrialized'), promoting tricuspid regurgitation, right atrial enlargement, and a high prevalence of accessory atrioventricular pathways.
official_outline_path: Embryonic development, fetal maturation, and perinatal transitional changes
Congenital disorders involving chambers and valves
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Abnormal neural crest migration causes conotruncal defects such as persistent truncus arteriosus and contributes to tetralogy of Fallot, not apical displacement of the tricuspid valve.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Failure of endocardial cushion fusion causes atrioventricular septal defects with abnormalities of the AV septum and common/abnormal AV valves, not atrialization of the right ventricle from a displaced tricuspid valve.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Excessive septum-primum resorption or inadequate septum-secundum development can produce a secundum atrial septal defect but does not cause tricuspid-leaflet displacement.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. The echocardiographic finding of apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet with an 'atrialized' proximal right ventricle is diagnostic of Ebstein anomaly. The developmental lesion is failure of normal delamination of the tricuspid valve leaflets—especially the septal and posterior leaflets—from the right ventricular myocardium. Poor leaflet coaptation causes tricuspid regurgitation and marked right atrial enlargement. Accessory atrioventricular pathways are common, explaining the ventricular preexcitation pattern in this patient.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Persistent ductus arteriosus is failure of postnatal ductal closure and creates an aortopulmonary shunt rather than a displaced tricuspid valve.

explanation.educational_objective: Explain Ebstein anomaly as failed delamination and apical displacement of the tricuspid valve, producing atrialization of the proximal right ventricle, tricuspid regurgitation, and susceptibility to accessory-pathway tachyarrhythmias.
explanation.key_explanation: The echocardiographic finding of apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet with an 'atrialized' proximal right ventricle is diagnostic of Ebstein anomaly. The developmental lesion is failure of normal delamination of the tricuspid valve leaflets—especially the septal and posterior leaflets—from the right ventricular myocardium. Poor leaflet coaptation causes tricuspid regurgitation and marked right atrial enlargement. Accessory atrioventricular pathways are common, explaining the ventricular preexcitation pattern in this patient.

item.vignette: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for episodic palpitations and mild exertional cyanosis. Cardiac examination shows a holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. ECG during sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a delta wave. Echocardiography shows severe tricuspid regurgitation, marked right atrial enlargement, and a tricuspid valve whose septal leaflet inserts abnormally far toward the right ventricular apex. A portion of the proximal right ventricle functions as part of the right atrium.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0609_Q0633_202609.claim: Abnormal neural crest migration causing defective separation of the aorta and pulmonary trunk is incorrect for this vignette. Abnormal neural crest migration causes conotruncal defects such as persistent truncus arteriosus and contributes to tetralogy of Fallot, not apical displacement of the tricuspid valve.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0609_Q0633_202609.target_mechanism: Failure of normal delamination of the septal and posterior tricuspid valve leaflets from the right ventricular myocardium causes apical displacement of the valve. The proximal portion of the right ventricle becomes functionally incorporated into the right atrium ('atrialized'), promoting tricuspid regurgitation, right atrial enlargement, and a high prevalence of accessory atrioventricular pathways.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0609_Q0633_202609.claim: Failure of normal delamination of tricuspid valve leaflets from the right ventricular myocardium is the uniquely best answer. The echocardiographic finding of apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet with an 'atrialized' proximal right ventricle is diagnostic of Ebstein anomaly. The developmental lesion is failure of normal delamination of the tricuspid valve leaflets—especially the septal and posterior leaflets—from the right ventricular myocardium. Poor leaflet coaptation causes tricuspid regurgitation and marked right atrial enlargement. Accessory atrioventricular pathways are common, explaining the ventricular preexcitation pattern in this patient.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Whipple disease — Tropheryma whipplei is phagocytosed by intestinal macrophages in susceptible hosts but is not effectively cleared. PAS-positive organism-laden macrophages accumulate in the small-intestinal lamina propria, distort villous architecture and function, and cause malabsorption; systemic spread can involve joints, heart, and central nervous system.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. This is the mechanism of celiac disease. Celiac enteropathy can cause villous atrophy and malabsorption, but it does not produce the characteristic PAS-positive foamy macrophages containing Tropheryma whipplei.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Disseminated MAC can involve gastrointestinal macrophages, especially with profound cellular immunodeficiency, but the organisms are acid-fast. The biopsy here is acid-fast negative and the migratory-arthralgia/Whipple pattern is different.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. The combination of migratory arthralgias that precede gastrointestinal symptoms, chronic malabsorption, and PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the small-intestinal lamina propria is classic for Whipple disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei. The organism is taken up by macrophages but persists intracellularly; accumulation of infected macrophages in the lamina propria disrupts normal villous structure and function, reducing nutrient absorption. The organisms are not acid-fast, which helps distinguish this pattern from mycobacterial infection.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Giardia trophozoites adhere to proximal small-bowel mucosa and can cause malabsorption, but histology does not characteristically show lamina-propria macrophages packed with PAS-positive bacterial material.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Primary intestinal lymphangiectasia causes dilated lymphatics, protein-losing enteropathy, and impaired chylomicron absorption rather than PAS-positive organism-laden macrophages.

explanation.educational_objective: Explain Whipple disease malabsorption as small-intestinal lamina-propria infiltration by PAS-positive Tropheryma whipplei–laden macrophages and distinguish it from celiac disease, disseminated MAC, giardiasis, and intestinal lymphangiectasia.
explanation.key_explanation: The combination of migratory arthralgias that precede gastrointestinal symptoms, chronic malabsorption, and PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the small-intestinal lamina propria is classic for Whipple disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei. The organism is taken up by macrophages but persists intracellularly; accumulation of infected macrophages in the lamina propria disrupts normal villous structure and function, reducing nutrient absorption. The organisms are not acid-fast, which helps distinguish this pattern from mycobacterial infection.

item.difficulty_basis: Requires separating Whipple disease from celiac disease, MAC, giardiasis, and intestinal lymphangiectasia by histology and systemic clues.
item.lead_in: Which process most directly explains this patient’s intestinal malabsorption?

options.A: CD4+ T-cell responses to deamidated gliadin presented by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, causing immune-mediated villous injury
options.B: Disseminated acid-fast Mycobacterium avium complex infection of intestinal macrophages in severe cellular immunodeficiency

item.vignette: A 52-year-old man has 2 years of intermittent migratory arthralgias followed by 6 months of chronic diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and unintentional weight loss. Laboratory studies show anemia and hypoalbuminemia. Upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy shows blunted villi and numerous foamy macrophages filling the lamina propria. The macrophages contain coarse periodic acid-Schiff–positive material, and an acid-fast stain is negative.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta — Heterozygous pathogenic THRB variants commonly produce a dominant-negative thyroid hormone receptor beta with reduced transcriptional response to T3. Resistance within the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis blunts normal negative feedback, so free T4/T3 are elevated while TSH remains inappropriately normal or elevated.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Activating TSH-receptor signaling causes autonomous hyperthyroidism with suppression of pituitary TSH, unlike the repeatedly nonsuppressed TSH in this family.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma can also produce high free T4/T3 with nonsuppressed TSH, but a normal pituitary MRI plus an autosomal-dominant family pattern across generations strongly supports inherited RTHβ instead.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. This pattern is resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ). Pathogenic THRB variants reduce tissue responsiveness to thyroid hormone and commonly act in a dominant-negative fashion. Because TRβ is important in hypothalamic and pituitary feedback, elevated circulating T4 and T3 fail to suppress TSH appropriately. Patients can be clinically near-euthyroid because thyroid hormone sensitivity varies among tissues. A familial pattern with persistently high free T4/T3, nonsuppressed TSH, exclusion of assay artifact, and no pituitary tumor strongly supports RTHβ.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased TBG elevates total T4/T3 while free hormone and TSH are generally normal; the vignette specifies repeatedly elevated free hormone concentrations.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Thyroid peroxidase loss impairs thyroid hormone synthesis and causes hypothyroidism with elevated TSH, the opposite biochemical pattern.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Nephronophthisis — Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive renal ciliopathy. Defects in nephrocystin and related ciliary proteins disrupt tubular epithelial signaling, producing impaired urinary concentration, chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis/fibrosis, tubular basement-membrane abnormalities, and later corticomedullary cyst formation.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Type IV collagen defects cause Alport-spectrum glomerular basement-membrane disease with hematuria and often hearing/ocular findings, not the bland tubulointerstitial concentrating-defect pattern shown.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. This is nephronophthisis, an autosomal recessive ciliopathy and important inherited cause of kidney failure in children and young adults. Defects in NPHP genes impair proteins localized to primary cilia and related ciliary structures in renal tubular epithelial cells. The earliest clinical clue is often reduced urine-concentrating ability, producing polyuria and polydipsia. Progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis causes anemia, growth impairment, and declining kidney function; imaging later may show small-to-normal kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation and corticomedullary cysts.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Nephrin/slit-diaphragm defects cause severe glomerular protein leakage, classically congenital nephrotic syndrome, rather than polyuria with little proteinuria and corticomedullary cysts.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Defective lysosomal cystine export causes cystinosis and proximal tubular Fanconi syndrome with generalized solute wasting, not the characteristic nephronophthisis phenotype.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. V2-receptor dysfunction causes X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with impaired concentrating ability, but does not cause chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis, anemia, progressive kidney failure, and corticomedullary cysts.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Osmotic demyelination syndrome — During chronic hyponatremia, brain cells adapt by losing inorganic ions and organic osmolytes to limit cerebral edema. If extracellular tonicity then rises too quickly during correction, osmolyte-depleted cells cannot restore intracellular solute rapidly enough; water leaves the cells, producing osmotic cellular injury, blood-brain-barrier/glial dysfunction, and noninflammatory demyelination, classically in the central pons.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronic hyponatremia triggers loss—not continued accumulation—of intracellular osmolytes as an adaptation against swelling. The danger arises when extracellular tonicity is then raised faster than brain cells can reacquire osmolytes.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. The patient has osmotic demyelination syndrome. In chronic hyponatremia, brain cells defend against swelling by extruding electrolytes and then organic osmolytes. This adaptation lowers intracellular osmotic content. If serum tonicity rises abruptly during treatment, extracellular fluid becomes relatively hypertonic before brain cells can replenish their osmolytes; water moves out of cells and causes osmotic injury to glial/myelin units. The central pons is especially susceptible, although extrapontine sites may also be affected. Modern evidence implicates early astrocyte injury as part of the cascade, so the mechanism should not be reduced to isolated oligodendrocyte shrinkage.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Postinfectious immune-mediated demyelination can occur in acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, but the temporal relationship to correction of chronic hyponatremia and the classic central pontine pattern indicate osmotic rather than autoimmune injury.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Alcohol use and malnutrition raise concern for Wernicke encephalopathy, but thiamine deficiency preferentially affects mammillary bodies, medial thalami and periaqueductal regions and does not explain delayed central pontine demyelination after sodium correction.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Basilar perforator ischemia can cause pontine deficits, but the symmetric central lesion appearing days after rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia is the classic nonvascular pattern of osmotic demyelination.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Plaque psoriasis driven by the IL-23/IL-17 axis — Activated dendritic cells and other innate immune cells produce IL-23, which sustains IL-17-producing T-cell populations. IL-17A and related cytokines act on keratinocytes to drive hyperproliferation, impaired differentiation, chemokine and antimicrobial-peptide production, and neutrophil recruitment, creating a self-amplifying inflammatory circuit.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. This is plaque psoriasis. A central pathogenic circuit is the IL-23/IL-17 axis. IL-23 supports expansion and maintenance of IL-17-producing lymphocytes; IL-17A then acts strongly on keratinocytes, inducing proliferation, abnormal differentiation, antimicrobial peptides, cytokines, and chemokines that recruit additional inflammatory cells, including neutrophils. This feed-forward loop explains acanthosis, parakeratosis, and neutrophilic aggregates such as Munro microabscesses. The importance of this pathway is also reflected by the effectiveness of IL-17- and IL-23-targeted therapies.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Th2/IL-4/IL-13 signaling is central to atopic dermatitis biology, not the dominant IL-23/IL-17 inflammatory circuit of plaque psoriasis.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. IFN-gamma–activated macrophages participate in granulomatous inflammation, but psoriasis is characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation and T17/neutrophilic inflammation rather than caseating dermal granulomas.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. IL-5/eosinophil and IgE/mast-cell pathways are typical of type I allergic/eosinophilic responses and do not explain the psoriatic histology.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. TGF-beta can promote fibrosis, but plaque psoriasis is not a fibrosing replacement disorder; its epidermal thickening reflects accelerated keratinocyte proliferation and abnormal differentiation.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Mixed connective tissue disease — Mixed connective tissue disease is a systemic autoimmune overlap syndrome strongly associated with high-titer anti-U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1-RNP) antibodies. The U1 snRNP is a component of the spliceosome that recognizes the 5′ splice site of pre-mRNA and participates in intron removal during mRNA maturation.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. The clinical overlap of Raynaud phenomenon, puffy hands, inflammatory arthritis, and myositis together with high-titer anti-U1-RNP antibodies supports mixed connective tissue disease. U1-RNP is part of the U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle in the spliceosome. U1 snRNP recognizes the 5′ splice site of precursor mRNA and helps assemble the spliceosomal complex that removes introns during RNA maturation. This item therefore links the defining serologic marker of MCTD to the normal molecular function of its autoantigen.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Origin licensing and replicative-helicase loading are DNA-replication functions of origin-recognition/licensing complexes, not U1 snRNP.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNA; some are autoimmune targets in inflammatory myopathies, but U1-RNP is a spliceosomal ribonucleoprotein.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Signal-recognition particle directs nascent secretory proteins to the rough ER; it is distinct from U1 snRNP.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome mediate regulated protein degradation, not splice-site recognition.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. A 50% relative reduction is mathematically correct but, without baseline absolute risk, can exaggerate perceived benefit; it also incorrectly implies that half of treated people personally avoid the outcome.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Left atrial myxoma with IL-6-mediated constitutional syndrome — Atrial myxomas are benign primary cardiac tumors that most often arise from the left atrium near the interatrial septum/fossa ovalis. Their mobility can cause intermittent mitral inflow obstruction and systemic embolization. Tumor-cell secretion of interleukin-6 drives many constitutional manifestations and acute-phase responses.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Histamine can mediate flushing, pruritus, and anaphylactoid symptoms, but it is not the characteristic cytokine responsible for the constitutional and acute-phase syndrome of atrial myxoma.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Ectopic erythropoietin causes erythrocytosis in selected tumors such as renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma; it does not explain the inflammatory syndrome of atrial myxoma.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. PTH-related peptide causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, not the typical fever, weight loss, elevated ESR, and CRP associated with cardiac myxoma.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. The pedunculated left atrial mass attached near the fossa ovalis, positional obstructive symptoms, and variable diastolic 'tumor plop' identify an atrial myxoma. Myxoma cells can actively secrete IL-6. Circulating IL-6 stimulates hepatic acute-phase protein production and contributes to fever, malaise, weight loss, arthralgias, and elevated inflammatory markers. IL-6 concentrations and constitutional findings commonly fall after complete tumor resection.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Serotonin secretion is characteristic of carcinoid tumors and can cause flushing, diarrhea, and right-sided valvular fibrosis; atrial myxoma does not produce its constitutional syndrome through serotonin.

explanation.educational_objective: Recognize IL-6 secretion by atrial myxoma cells as the basis of the constitutional and acute-phase syndrome accompanying this otherwise histologically benign cardiac tumor.
explanation.key_explanation: The pedunculated left atrial mass attached near the fossa ovalis, positional obstructive symptoms, and variable diastolic 'tumor plop' identify an atrial myxoma. Myxoma cells can actively secrete IL-6. Circulating IL-6 stimulates hepatic acute-phase protein production and contributes to fever, malaise, weight loss, arthralgias, and elevated inflammatory markers. IL-6 concentrations and constitutional findings commonly fall after complete tumor resection.

item.tested_construct: Atrial myxomas are benign primary cardiac tumors that most often arise from the left atrium near the interatrial septum/fossa ovalis. Their mobility can cause intermittent mitral inflow obstruction and systemic embolization. Tumor-cell secretion of interleukin-6 drives many constitutional manifestations and acute-phase responses.
item.vignette: A 46-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue, low-grade fevers, weight loss, and intermittent exertional dyspnea that is worse when she lies in certain positions. Examination reveals a low-pitched diastolic sound after S2 that varies with body position. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are elevated. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated mass attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis that intermittently prolapses through the mitral valve.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Adult granulosa cell tumor of the ovary — Granulosa cell tumors retain normal granulosa-cell steroidogenic functions. FSH signaling induces aromatase (CYP19A1) in granulosa cells, allowing conversion of theca-derived androgens to estrogens. Estrogen excess from a granulosa cell tumor can stimulate the endometrium and cause abnormal uterine bleeding or endometrial hyperplasia.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Theca interna cells respond primarily to LH and generate androgen substrate, but the tumor derives from granulosa cells and the endometrial effect results from granulosa-cell estrogen production.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. 5-alpha-reductase generates dihydrotestosterone in androgen-responsive tissues and does not explain estrogen excess from an ovarian granulosa cell tumor.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase is an adrenal steroidogenic enzyme and is unrelated to the ovarian estrogen-producing phenotype shown here.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. The ovarian tumor is an adult granulosa cell tumor, identified by Call-Exner bodies, nuclear grooves, and inhibin positivity. Granulosa cells normally express FSH receptors. FSH increases aromatase activity, enabling granulosa cells to convert androstenedione produced by LH-stimulated theca cells into estrogens. Granulosa cell tumors can preserve this steroidogenic phenotype and produce excess estrogen, which stimulates endometrial proliferation and can cause postmenopausal bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Leydig cells can convert cholesterol to steroid precursors under LH stimulation, but they are not the cell of origin of this ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor.

explanation.educational_objective: Link the hyperestrogenic presentation of a granulosa cell tumor to normal granulosa-cell physiology: FSH-induced aromatization of theca-derived androgen substrate.

Granulosa cells normally express FSH receptors. FSH increases aromatase activity, enabling granulosa cells to convert androstenedione produced by LH-stimulated theca cells into estrogens. Granulosa cell tumors can preserve this steroidogenic phenotype and produce excess estrogen, which stimulates endometrial proliferation and can cause postmenopausal bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia.

item.vignette: A 58-year-old woman who completed menopause 6 years ago presents with new uterine bleeding. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a unilateral ovarian mass and a thickened endometrium. Endometrial biopsy shows simple hyperplasia without atypia. The ovarian mass is resected; histology shows small uniform cells with grooved nuclei surrounding eosinophilic fluid-filled spaces consistent with Call-Exner bodies. Tumor cells stain for inhibin.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Physiologic neonatal jaundice — Normal newborns have a transiently limited capacity to conjugate bilirubin because hepatic UGT1A1 activity is developmentally immature. A higher red-cell mass, shorter erythrocyte lifespan, and increased enterohepatic circulation also raise bilirubin load, but immature conjugation is the developmental feature that directly limits hepatic clearance.
official_outline_path: Normal physiologic findings in the neonatal period
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Complete UGT1A1 absence causes severe pathologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia such as Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I, not mild self-limited jaundice in a well term infant.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Immune hemolysis increases bilirubin production and may cause early pathologic jaundice; the negative direct antiglobulin test and otherwise normal evaluation argue against this mechanism.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Extrahepatic biliary obstruction causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and may produce pale stools and dark urine, findings absent here.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. This infant has physiologic neonatal jaundice: mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia appearing after the first 24 hours in an otherwise healthy newborn. Newborns have increased bilirubin production from greater red-cell mass and shorter erythrocyte survival and also have increased enterohepatic circulation. However, the developmental feature that directly limits hepatic bilirubin clearance is immature UGT1A1 activity in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which transiently reduces conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Increased intestinal beta-glucuronidase can increase enterohepatic bilirubin circulation, but it does not directly limit hepatic conjugation; transiently low hepatic UGT1A1 activity does.

explanation.educational_objective: Recognize transiently reduced neonatal hepatic UGT1A1 conjugating capacity as the developmental limitation in physiologic unconjugated jaundice while distinguishing it from hemolysis, biliary obstruction, and inherited absence of UGT1A1.

However, the developmental feature that directly limits hepatic bilirubin clearance is immature UGT1A1 activity in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which transiently reduces conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid.

evidence_map.claim: Maternal IgG-mediated destruction of the infant’s erythrocytes: Incorrect. Immune hemolysis increases bilirubin production and may cause early pathologic jaundice; the negative direct antiglobulin test and otherwise normal evaluation argue against this mechanism.

evidence_map.claim: Failure of bile flow from extrahepatic biliary obstruction: Incorrect. Extrahepatic biliary obstruction causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and may produce pale stools and dark urine, findings absent here.

evidence_map.claim: Transiently low activity of hepatic bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1): Correct. This infant has physiologic neonatal jaundice: mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia appearing after the first 24 hours in an otherwise healthy newborn. Newborns have increased bilirubin production from greater red-cell mass and shorter erythrocyte survival and also have increased enterohepatic circulation. However, the developmental feature that directly limits hepatic bilirubin clearance is immature UGT1A1 activity in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which transiently reduces conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Atheroembolic renal disease (cholesterol crystal embolization) — Disruption of advanced atherosclerotic plaques, often after aortic or arterial instrumentation, releases cholesterol crystals that lodge in small renal arteries and arterioles. Partial luminal obstruction plus a secondary inflammatory/giant-cell reaction causes subacute ischemic kidney injury; systemic microembolization can produce livedo reticularis or blue toes while distal pulses remain palpable.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute tubular injury can follow iodinated contrast exposure, but it does not explain the delayed systemic microembolic skin findings, eosinophilia, and small-vessel cholesterol-crystal lesions characteristic of atheroembolism.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. A large thromboembolus to a main renal arterial branch causes a renal infarction pattern rather than diffuse cholesterol microembolization with blue toes and livedo while pulses remain present.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Immune-complex glomerulonephritis produces glomerular inflammatory findings and active urine sediment; it does not explain cholesterol embolization after vascular instrumentation.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Oxalate nephropathy produces intratubular calcium oxalate deposition and has a different metabolic or toxic exposure context.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. The delayed kidney injury after angiography together with blue toes, livedo reticularis, eosinophilia, and preserved distal pulses is classic for cholesterol crystal embolization. Instrumentation can disrupt an aortic atherosclerotic plaque, releasing cholesterol crystals that shower small arteries and arterioles in the kidneys and other organs. During tissue processing, cholesterol dissolves and leaves elongated needle-shaped or biconvex clefts within vessel lumina, often surrounded by an inflammatory and giant-cell reaction.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria — The classic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a cold-reactive biphasic IgG autoantibody, usually directed against the P blood-group antigen. It binds RBCs and fixes complement at lower temperatures in peripheral tissues; when blood returns to 37°C, the antibody dissociates while complement activation proceeds to intravascular hemolysis.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Cold agglutinin disease is classically mediated by IgM, often anti-I, with complement fixation; it is mechanistically distinct from the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner IgG antibody of PCH.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is mediated by warm-reactive IgG and predominantly splenic extravascular hemolysis; the C3-only DAT and positive Donath-Landsteiner test point elsewhere.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-induced hemoglobin denaturation and bite-cell/Heinz-body hemolysis rather than a complement-positive immune hemolysis.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. PNH results from a PIGA-mutant hematopoietic clone lacking GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55/CD59, producing chronic/acquired complement-mediated hemolysis rather than a transient postinfectious Donath-Landsteiner syndrome.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. This child has paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, an acute autoimmune hemolytic anemia that often follows infection in children. The classic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG autoantibody, usually anti-P. It binds erythrocytes and fixes complement in cooler peripheral blood, then dissociates as blood is rewarmed while complement activation continues, producing intravascular hemolysis. Because IgG can detach before testing, the DAT often detects complement (C3) without IgG.

explanation.educational_objective: Distinguish paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria from cold agglutinin disease and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia by recognizing the biphasic IgG anti-P Donath-Landsteiner mechanism.

The classic Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG autoantibody, usually anti-P. It binds erythrocytes and fixes complement in cooler peripheral blood, then dissociates as blood is rewarmed while complement activation continues, producing intravascular hemolysis. Because IgG can detach before testing, the DAT often detects complement (C3) without IgG.

item.lead_in: Which mechanism best explains this patient’s hemolysis?

options.A: A cold-reactive IgM antibody cross-links the I antigen and causes predominantly complement-mediated extravascular hemolysis in the liver

options.C: Oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin in erythrocytes with deficient glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
options.D: Loss of GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59 permits uncontrolled complement attack on a clonal population of erythrocytes
options.E: A cold-reactive IgG antibody binds the P antigen and fixes complement at low temperature; complement-mediated lysis occurs after the blood is rewarmed
